```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5)
```

Every other walk-through recovers a parameter from a price the studio *set*. Here
the price is what a buyer and a seller agreed on — an **equilibrium outcome**. You
cannot randomize it, only the things that shift it, and (price, quantity) pairs
alone trace neither curve (the simultaneity problem). The data is a panel of
weekly market equilibria over differentiated goods (cards) grouped into nests by
quality × role; demand is a nested logit, so the object we report is a
**diversion matrix**, not a scalar elasticity.

Identification comes from the content calendar: a **pack promo** injects stock (a
supply shifter — traces demand) and an **SBC** raises a card's utility (a demand
shifter). Randomizing which cards each event touches turns them into instruments.
Estimator: the Berry (1994) inversion, by OLS (biased) and by 2SLS (identified),
with standard errors **clustered by week** — one week's goods trade against a
shared denominator, so they are not independent.

# 1. Data

```{r data}
library(AER)        # ivreg
library(sandwich)   # vcovCL — cluster-robust
library(lmtest)     # coeftest
library(ggplot2)

m <- read.csv("../data/market_panel.csv")     # observable: one row per good x week
truth <- read.csv("../data/market_truth.csv")
alpha_true  <- truth$value[truth$param == "alpha_true"]
lambda_true <- truth$value[truth$param == "lambda_true"]

# Berry LHS and the within-nest share regressor
m$y      <- log(m$s_j) - log(m$s0)
m$ln_sjg <- log(m$s_jg)

# BLP-style rival instruments: same-nest rivals hit by a promo / SBC this week
m$nest_promo <- ave(m$promo, m$week, m$nest, FUN = sum) - m$promo
m$nest_sbc   <- ave(m$sbc,   m$week, m$nest, FUN = sum) - m$sbc
head(m[, c("week", "good", "nest", "logp", "q", "s_j", "promo", "sbc")])
```

The Berry inversion is linear in the parameters:

$$\ln s_j - \ln s_0 \;=\; b_0 + \beta x_j + c\,\text{SBC}_j \;-\;\alpha\,\log p_j \;+\;(1-\lambda)\ln s_{j\mid g} \;+\;\xi_j$$

Two regressors are endogenous: $\log p_j$ (price is an equilibrium outcome,
correlated with the unobserved demand shock $\xi_j$) and $\ln s_{j\mid g}$ (a
share, mechanically correlated with $\xi_j$). Recover $\alpha = -\,\text{coef}(\log p)$
and $\lambda = 1 - \text{coef}(\ln s_{j\mid g})$.

# 2. Why the raw scatter traces nothing

```{r scatter}
ggplot(m, aes(logp, log(q), color = factor(promo))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("0" = "grey60", "1" = "#c0392b"),
                     labels = c("no promo", "pack promo"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "log price", y = "log quantity",
       title = "Equilibria, not a demand curve — until a shifter separates them")
```

Promo weeks (a supply shock) push a good down-and-right along its demand curve;
demand shocks push up-and-right along supply. The cloud is the mixture. Only an
instrument recovers a slope from it.

# 3. The problem: naive OLS Berry inversion

```{r ols}
ols <- lm(y ~ x + sbc + logp + ln_sjg, data = m)
ols_cl <- coeftest(ols, vcov = vcovCL, cluster = m$week)   # cluster by week
alpha_ols <- -coef(ols)["logp"]; lam_ols <- 1 - coef(ols)["ln_sjg"]
c(alpha_ols = alpha_ols, lam_ols = lam_ols)
```

The demand shock moves both price and the shares, so the price coefficient is
pulled hard toward zero — the market version of "we raised prices and sold more."

# 4. The fix — 2SLS

Instrument the two endogenous regressors with the excluded shifters: own **promo**
(a pure supply shock, excluded from demand) plus the same-nest rival promo / SBC
counts (they reach good $j$ only through equilibrium prices).

```{r iv}
iv <- ivreg(y ~ x + sbc + logp + ln_sjg |
              x + sbc + promo + nest_promo + nest_sbc, data = m)
iv_cl <- coeftest(iv, vcov = vcovCL, cluster = m$week)   # cluster by week
alpha_iv <- -coef(iv)["logp"]; lam_iv <- 1 - coef(iv)["ln_sjg"]
iv_cl[c("logp", "ln_sjg"), ]
```

```{r diagnostics}
# first stage strength for the price equation (weak-IV guard: clear ~10 by a lot)
summary(iv, diagnostics = TRUE)$diagnostics
```

# 5. Validate against the oracle

```{r validate}
se_alpha_iv <- iv_cl["logp", "Std. Error"]        # SE of coef(logp) == SE of alpha
res <- data.frame(
  estimator = c("OLS", "2SLS"),
  alpha_hat = c(alpha_ols, alpha_iv),
  lam_hat   = c(lam_ols,   lam_iv)
)
res$alpha_bias <- res$alpha_hat - alpha_true
res$lam_bias   <- res$lam_hat   - lambda_true
res$ci_covers_alpha <- abs(res$alpha_hat - alpha_true) <=
  1.96 * c(ols_cl["logp", "Std. Error"], se_alpha_iv)
res
```

OLS is badly attenuated on $\alpha$; 2SLS recovers both $\alpha$ (truth
`r round(alpha_true,2)`) and $\lambda$ (truth `r round(lambda_true,2)`) and its
95% CI covers the truth. $\lambda < 1$ *is* the substitution structure — the next
section makes it a matrix.

# 6. The object that matters: the diversion matrix

With thousands of differentiated goods the own-price elasticity of one card is
close to meaningless — buyers choose among substitutes. The reported object is the
**diversion matrix**: of the demand a good loses when its price rises, where does
it go. We evaluate the true and recovered demand systems at one common set of
reference prices (the oracle `market_reference.csv`, cleared at truth), so the
comparison isolates demand-parameter error.

```{r nl-helpers}
# nested-logit shares and a numeric diversion matrix — the same algebra as
# src/demand_sim/market.py, kept raw here so it can be read inline.
nl_shares <- function(delta, nest, lam) {
  groups <- sort(unique(nest))
  Dgl <- sapply(groups, function(g) sum(exp(delta[nest == g] / lam))^lam)
  denom <- 1 + sum(Dgl)
  s <- numeric(length(delta)); sjg <- numeric(length(delta))
  for (i in seq_along(groups)) {
    idx <- nest == groups[i]
    e <- exp(delta[idx] / lam); Dg <- sum(e)
    s[idx]   <- (e / Dg) * (Dgl[i] / denom)
    sjg[idx] <- e / Dg
  }
  list(s = s, s0 = 1 / denom, sjg = sjg)
}

diversion <- function(delta, nest, lam, alpha, eps = 1e-4) {
  base <- nl_shares(delta, nest, lam)$s
  J <- length(delta); D <- matrix(0, J, J)
  for (j in seq_len(J)) {
    d2 <- delta; d2[j] <- d2[j] - alpha * eps       # a small price bump on j
    b <- nl_shares(d2, nest, lam)$s
    loss <- base[j] - b[j]; g <- b - base; g[j] <- 0
    if (loss > 0) D[j, ] <- g / loss
  }
  D
}
```

```{r diversion}
ref <- read.csv("../data/market_reference.csv")     # ORACLE reference prices
delta_true <- ref$mean_util - alpha_true * ref$logp_ref
delta_hat  <- ref$mean_util - alpha_iv   * ref$logp_ref
D_true <- diversion(delta_true, ref$nest, lambda_true, alpha_true)
D_hat  <- diversion(delta_hat,  ref$nest, lam_iv,      alpha_iv)

off  <- !diag(nrow(D_true))
same <- outer(ref$nest, ref$nest, `==`)
c(diversion_mae = mean(abs(D_true[off] - D_hat[off])),
  within_nest_share_true = sum(D_true[off & same]) / sum(D_true[off]),
  within_nest_share_hat  = sum(D_hat[off & same])  / sum(D_hat[off]))
```

```{r diversion-heatmap, fig.height=5}
long <- expand.grid(loses = seq_len(nrow(D_hat)), gains = seq_len(ncol(D_hat)))
long$diversion <- as.vector(D_hat)   # R is column-major: row (loses) varies fastest
ggplot(long, aes(gains, loses, fill = diversion)) + geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma") + scale_y_reverse() +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Recovered diversion matrix — mass concentrates within nests",
       x = "demand gained by card", y = "card that raised its price")
```

Substitution is fierce inside a nest and weak across — the block structure is
visible, and the recovered within-nest share matches the oracle to a fraction of a
percent. That is the payoff the note asked for: not a scalar elasticity argued for
from a scatter, but a substitution structure recovered *through a market that
clears*, and graded against a truth we generated.

# 7. Note — no Phase 5 forecast here

The other walk-throughs end with a demand forecast. Phase 6 estimates a *static
demand system*, so the terminal object is the diversion matrix, not a time-series
forecast. The forecasting arc resumes when the order book lands (docs/10 §6): the
listing-level survival curve is a demand read the aggregated panel cannot give,
and bunching at price bands is a second censoring channel on top of the inventory
censoring of Phases 2 and 5.
